newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - John Hancock eyes acquisitions.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - John Hancock eyes acquisitions.

text.p: John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance Co is interested in expanding its core retail life insurance and long-term care businesses by making an acquisition outside its East Coast stronghold.

John Hancock chief financial officer Tom Moloney, speaking to Reuters in a telephone interview last week, said the company also might use the proceeds from recent non-core asset sales to acquire an asset management business. But the Boston-based financial services firm is not holding talks with potential candidates at the moment.

"Because of the way the landscape is changing so quickly, the major focus is really on the retail area and looking at distribution; and the possibility of acquiring additional distribution, probably targeted more on a geographic basis than anything else," he said.
And if the target company has strong management and a good franchise value, then Hancock might prefer to keep the operation in place rather than breaking it down and consolidating it into Hancock.
"We're pretty flexible in talking to people about what their needs are as well as our own," he said.

John Hancock, the country's ninth largest life insurance company, earlier this year completed the sale of its group health and related life insurance businesses to WellPoint Health Networks Inc for about $86.7 million. And late last year, Hancock completed the sale of Freedom Securities to Freedom's management and outside equity partners for $180 million.
Hancock also sold its Hancock Venture Partners Inc to the Venture Partners management earlier this year, but financial terms were not disclosed.
"We're now out looking for ways of investing those dollars, either through acquisition or other opportunities that we have to grow the core businesses that we have," Moloney said.
And finding ways to boost growth is the most important issue facing the company, even more critical than increasing its financial flexibility.

"That to me is really the major initiative," he said. "If I were to lay awake at night thinking of things, that's the one. Because of the actions we've taken over the last five to six months with our (asset) sales, capital isn't the major issue right at this very moment."

But as a mutual, John Hancock is owned by its policyholders and is therefore unable to raise capital by issuing stock. And that could hamper its ability to compete against publicly-traded companies in the future.

John Hancock has been one of the major forces behind an effort to reform Massachusetts law to allow mutual insurers to convert into mutual holding companies that can then own publicly-traded insurance subsidiaries.
About 10 other states now allow mutual holding companies.

Such a move would help make mutuals more competitive with public companies by giving them the ability raise capital through a stock offering and the opportunity to use their stock as currency in any merger transactions. In addition, that option would be a lot less costly than going through a full demutualization.
A demutualization -- in which a mutual converts to a stock company -- was considered by Hancock in the past and Moloney said he would not rule one out in the future.
"I would never rule anything out. I think it's probably slightly better than 50/50 that we'd end up considering a demutualization," he said.
"But that's something that's down the road a ways," he added, noting that the company currently has sufficient capital to pursue its strategic objectives.
The company also has considered spinning off a minority stake of one or more of its asset management operations to better realize the market value of the businesses.
"That's one of the things we've looked at in the past and have that as one of the alternatives if some others don't work out," he said.
